title: Hitch your wagon to a star
word: Hitch your wagon to a star
hookLine: aim high and let greater forces carry you (Civilization)

cards: Nobody is turning the millstone. Grain gets ground all afternoon beside the river, because the water is falling anyway and the wheel only has to catch it.
Out on the lake, nobody rows the sailboat either; the wind fills the sail while the person at the tiller mostly just steers.

Emerson reached for pictures like these, and out of them came a line that turns up on posters: hitch your wagon to a star. It's easy to read it as dream big. Emerson meant something a little different.

teach.b: First, where it comes from: an essay called Civilization, in a passage about how people get great work done.
Emerson's answer: not mostly by muscle, but by borrowing forces far bigger than ourselves. The wind, the falling water, the weight of the earth. Second, the wagon.

"Hitch your wagon to a star," he writes, and the wise worker then sees the chore done by the gods themselves. The work still gets done, but the pulling comes from something larger than the one doing it.
It's less about straining upward than about getting connected to the right power. Third, the catch. The great forces only help with certain kinds of work.

teach.h: NO GOD WILL HELP US LIE.
teach.b: Emerson warns against small, grabbing work that serves only ourselves: no god will help us lie and steal; their teams are all going the other way.

teach.h: A PLAIN WAGON, A HIGH STAR.
teach.b: So the star isn't just any high goal. He names the interests he says the gods honor: justice, love, freedom, knowledge, utility.

teach.h: HITCH YOUR WAGON TO A STAR.
teach.b: Hitch your work to those, and they pull. Fourth, an ordinary day. A high aim doesn't have to be a giant one.
Tell the truth in a hard meeting. Teach a child patiently. Make something that serves more than your own pocket.
The star is the direction. The wagon is your plain daily work, hitched to it.

how: Readers often quote this line from Emerson's Civilization as advice to aim high; read in context, it is about linking ordinary work to larger forces and to the good.

games.q: you've got a heavy wagon to move and you're tired. in Emerson's picture, what's the smart move?
o: hitch it to a star and let the larger forces pull.
leave the wagon where it is.
games.why: Emerson: "hitch your wagon to a star," and see the chore done by the gods themselves. the pulling comes from something larger.

practice: Ask what you'd most like your ordinary work to serve: not a title or a number, but a direction, like honesty, kindness, beauty, fairness or healing, and let one word rise.
Then picture one plain task from tomorrow, an email, a shift, a chore, hitched to that word and pulled by it.
